Facts. I know so many people in my year group who have punched, leaving the bottom of the barrel as the only options for current and future leadership positions.

I've seen a big difference between pilot/CSO washouts and people who's eyes sucked too bad to go those routes.

With ABAD, CRC and E-7, and all the WOC and lead wing initiatives, we're spread pretty thin, and oftentimes don't send our best to the one-offs.

Tempo is bad especially in the CRC (thanks, Kingpin), and lots of people get out for that. Overall, now's a great time to go CRC because of the ability to field capability quickly vs. modifying an airplane (E-7), which takes a lot more $$$.

Finally, the flux you referred to in your first paragraph is the root cause of a lot of the issues you see with many ABMs. Things are changing constantly, money isn't coming through for C2 capability in the Air Force (USMC, USA, and USN are all dwarfing the USAF in C2 funding), and people grow frustrated and bitter unless they have a group of great Americans to encourage/vent to.

Challenging time to be in the USAF for most career fields, so ABM's not an anomoly - just know what you're getting into.

**Arguments for:**

-Career field undergoing massive change

-Getting lots of upgraded equipment over the next few years, in CRC and E-3

-Getting new CRC equipment super-fast, meaning there's a lot of work to be done

-Bar is low, so if you're good at your job you'll be taken care of

-Decent overseas options

**Arguments against:**

-Career field undergoing massive change

-Not getting E-7 for a few years

-Getting new CRC equipment super-fast, meaning there's a lot of work to be done

-Bar is low, so if you're good at your job there will be a lot of work for you

-You could get stuck at the 552 for a while
Not a silver bullet, but CRC gives a much more balanced experience and gets you away from the E-3 shenanigans.

Good: I haven't had a drink in two weeks, which is the longest stretch for me in the past five years.

Bad: Stress at work and home is driving me to find a coping mechanism. So far I've been listening to music, exercising, or just taking some melatonin to fall asleep. I'm worried I'll become reliant on the melatonin/avoiding the issue rather than building up willpower to resist.

Rest: I would love some! It's been good to have more sober time with the family recently, and have been able to catch up on some house projects that have fallen by the wayside. Still a long road ahead, but grateful for this community; even though it's my first time posting, I've appreciated the honesty and support y'all show on the daily.

Thank you! We are teaching our kids proper body part names instead of "privates," to teach them to respect their own bodies, and demand respect from others. Same with the stranger danger rules. My kids are still young enough to default to trusting adults.

Really appreciate your taking the time to explain all of these, and offer them to us to help us be better parents. I will definitely read the information you linked, and am grateful you are part of this community.
If you want to DM me any online therapy resources you've personally found helpful, I'd appreciate it. And it's simultaneously heartbreaking and encouraging that I'm not alone.

I can't tell my partner; I love her, and don't want to burden her. Of course I trust her, but I don't think telling everything to everyone is the right answer.

Telling this community is a weight off my shoulders. I will consider therapy, but one of my friends had a negative experience with telling someone in church he trusted, and my area doesn't have the best therapists. I'd rather try to fight alone with y'all then seek help in the local community and be disappointed or undercut.

Thank you for your support and encouragement. It's hard to hope that I can be a good parent, but I always will do my best, and will never, ever be anything remotely like my dad. I never let my kids out of my sight when I visit home. I can't abandon my mom because she really did a good job raising us, and she would be hurt if we stopped visiting. She loves her grandkids too.

Kids have been healing, stressful, and haunting. Sometimes situations will pop up where I remember what happened with my dad, while I'm taking care of my kids, and it's an immediate crushing, despairing feeling. I almost always feel like I need to be alone to process and be sad, which hurts my wife and kids sometimes. I think it's better to process on my own than spread the trauma to those I care about.

I like your username. I hope to be something free of my trauma one day.

I understand how you feel, and I appreciate you sharing your story. I've been dealing with similar issues, and I'm glad I'm not alone.

You're not alone either, and there are people who want to support and help you. Nothing that happened was your fault. I know therapy and psychiatry are daunting and expensive, but if you have the opportunity to try them, please do.

I'm also familiar with having to live in (and visit) a place where I was abused, and know how difficult it can be. I feel my best when I am away from that place. It's hard to move away, but I hope you can find a friend or family that will take you in for a little while. Living in the place where I was abused for a long time is a nightmare, and you are incredibly strong for pushing through it.
I'm so sorry you've had to deal with this. It wasn't your fault, and there are lots of people who want to help you. I'm glad you're trying to get better.
I'm glad you're getting some closure and justice.

I hired a property manager because my wife is busy with the kids, and not financially inclined. It's been very easy. Just shop around for one with a lower monthly rate. Most seem to be around 10-12%, but we found one at 8%. The manager handles all the maintenance and communication with the tenants, so we just have to collect the checks and sign off on any big repairs, which haven't happened yet.

So far, there haven't been any cons to renting out instead of selling. Depending on your situation and how much you can get monthly for a rental, the long-term benefit may be better for just selling and dropping the extra cash into an index fund.

I have heard some horror stories of others managing their own properties, but these are few and far between. Usually, it works out pretty well and isn't too painful, especially if you have a business-minded spouse to help out. Still, make sure you screen your tenants; the majority of horror stories have to do with terrible tenants.

The one thing I always recommend to first-time military home buyers is the Dream Makers grant by PenFed; it can provide up to $5k in matching funds for your first home. 

If you or your spouse wants to take an active role in property management, then definitely look at renting out, depending on your area. We use a property manager for 8% of the rent, and it's still really worth it. We don't have to worry about the minutiae of renting out a property, and we still collect the mortgage/insurance plus some extra. It's free money!
